title: How long is the line after more and more halvings?
description: A line sixteen units long is halved five times and ten times, and each length is written as a fraction and as a power of two. The video shows an exponent going below zero, and Keeko doubts whether a minus sign in the exponent makes the number negative.
teaching_notes: One idea: when more twos are below the bar than above, the exponent goes below zero and the power is a fraction. Watch for students who read two to the power negative one as minus two.

source: A line is 16 units long. Find its length after halving it 5 times and 10 times, as a fraction and as a power of 2.
video_script.why: A learner sees what the rule for dividing powers gives when the second exponent is larger, and why that is a fraction.
video_script.substitution: the book's own line of sixteen units, halved five times and ten times
video_script.anchor: a line of sixteen units drawn on the board and halved again and again
video_script.wrong_move: reads two to the power negative one as the number minus two
video_script.payoff_line: More twos below the bar than above leave a fraction

final_answer.value: 1/2 unit, which is 2 to the power −1, and 1/64 unit, which is 2 to the power −6
final_answer.spoken: one half unit, which is two to the power negative one, and one over sixty four unit, which is two to the power negative six

video_script.fraction_reading: 1/64 is read one over sixty four
video_script.design: One idea: more twos below than above gives a fraction. Wrong idea: the minus sign makes the number negative. The twos are drawn above and below the bar and the leftover twos land below; the fraction one over sixty four only appears at the answer.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; a line 16 units long that is halved again and again

marks.line: a line marked 16 units long is drawn
marks.half: half of the line is erased again and again, five times and then ten times
marks.ask: two empty boxes stand ready for the two lengths

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='line'/>A line is sixteen units long.
<bookmark mark='half'/>We erase half of it again and again. First we do it five times, and then ten times.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How long is the line left after five halvings, and after ten?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: 2^4 / 2^5 as a fraction: four 2s above the bar, five 2s below it, four pairs joined

marks.above: four 2s are drawn above the bar
marks.below: five 2s are drawn below the bar
marks.pairs: four pairs are joined and one 2 below has no partner

narration: <bookmark mark='above'/>Sixteen is four twos multiplied. Halving five times divides by five twos.
<bookmark mark='below'/>There are more twos below the bar than above it.
<bookmark mark='pairs'/>Each two above cancels one below, but a two below is left without a partner.

beats.on_screen: Given: a line of 16 units = 2^4 units, halved 5 times and 10 times

marks.given: the line of 16 units is written as 2^4 units

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a line of sixteen units, which is two to the power four. It is halved five times and ten times.

beats.on_screen: To find: each length as a fraction and as a power of 2

marks.find: the words each length as a fraction and as a power of 2 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find each length as a fraction, and as a power of two.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Step one, halve five times. That divides by two to the power five, which is thirty two.
<bookmark mark='frac'/>Sixteen divided by thirty two is one half of a unit.

marks.rule: 2^(4 - 5) is written from the rule for dividing powers

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step two, use the rule for dividing powers, which takes the exponents away.
<bookmark mark='neg'/>Four take away five is negative one, so the same division gives two to the power negative one.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Both ways give the same length, so two to the power negative one is one half.

beats.on_screen: 10 halvings: 2^4 / 2^10 = (2 x 2 x 2 x 2) / (ten 2s); four pairs cancel and six 2s are left below: 1/(2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2) = 1/2^6

marks.ten: 2^4 / 2^10 is written with four 2s above and ten 2s below
marks.cancel: four pairs cancel, and six 2s are left below the bar
marks.six: 1/(2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2) = 1/2^6 appears

narration: <bookmark mark='ten'/>Step three, halve ten times. That divides by ten twos, with only four twos above the bar.
<bookmark mark='cancel'/>Four pairs cancel, and six twos are left below the bar.
<bookmark mark='six'/>The length is one over six twos multiplied together. That is one over two to the power six.

marks.same: 2^-6 = 1/2^6 is joined with the result of the cancelling
marks.sixty: 2^6 = 64 is written, the fraction is left unsimplified

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step four, use the rule again. Four take away ten is negative six, which gives two to the power negative six.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Cancelling gave one over two to the power six, so the two forms match.
<bookmark mark='sixty'/>Two to the power six is sixty four.

marks.pay: the leftover twos below the bar are boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>More twos below the bar than above leave a fraction.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>After five halvings the line is one half unit, which is two to the power negative one.
<bookmark mark='ten'/>After ten halvings it is one over sixty four unit, which is two to the power negative six.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 2^-1 = -2, struck out; 1/2 unit beside it

marks.fix: the half unit line from step one appears beside the bubble
marks.all: the bubble is struck out and the 2 is moved below the bar

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks two to the power negative one is negative two, because of the minus sign.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But a line cannot have a negative length. Sixteen divided by thirty two is one half.
<bookmark mark='all'/>The minus sign in the exponent only says the two sits below the bar.
